messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Leilani was twenty years old and had been married for just under a year when she walked into my office, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, her eyes scanning the room before settling on the door. She was an interior designer for a small firm, a job she had once loved for the way it let her shape spaces into something safe and beautiful. Now, she could barely stand to be in a room alone. The trauma had happened six months ago, though she still struggled to tell the story in a straight line. When she tried, she would start, then lose the thread, her voice trailing off into silence, her face crumpling with frustration and guilt. What she could say was this: her husband, the man she had trusted most, had hurt her. It had happened at night, in their apartment, after an argument about something she could no longer remember. He had grabbed her by the shoulders and slammed her against the wall, then again, then shoved her to the floor. She had curled into a ball, and he had kicked her ribs until she stopped making noise. When it was over, he had cried and apologized, and she had told herself it was a mistake, that he loved her, that she must have done something to provoke it. That was the story she could not finish telling, because every time she reached the part where she stayed, the guilt rose up so thick it choked her.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani’s world shrank. She began to avoid being alone in any room, especially if it was dark. She would leave every light on in the apartment, even during the day, and she would follow her husband from room to room, not out of affection but out of a desperate, wordless fear that if she lost sight of him, something worse would happen. She could not explain why she felt safer near the man who had hurt her—only that being alone felt like being prey. At work, she found herself flinching at loud noises: a door slamming, a file cabinet dropping, a coworker’s laugh too sharp. She started taking lunch at her desk, avoiding the communal break room where men she did not know might walk in. She became hypervigilant in ways that exhausted her. Her body felt constantly tense, like a wire pulled too tight, ready to snap at any sound. She checked behind her when she walked down the hallway, certain someone was following her, even though she knew rationally that no one was.

The worst moments came without warning. Sometimes, in the middle of a quiet task—selecting fabric samples, measuring a window—she would be flooded with the full emotional intensity of that night: the terror, the helplessness, the shame. But there was no image, no clear memory attached. Just the feeling, raw and formless, as if it lived in her body and not her mind. Those episodes left her shaken and unable to explain to anyone what had happened. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by that night, that she no longer belonged anywhere—not at work, not with her family, not even in her own marriage. She had begun to feel that people could not be trusted, that everyone was capable of the same cruelty, and that she was foolish for ever believing otherwise.

What finally brought her to therapy was a moment of occupational consequence. She had been assigned to design a new office layout for a client, a project she would normally have loved. But the site visit required her to be alone in a dark, unfinished building with a male contractor. She canceled three times, then told her boss she could not do it, offering no explanation. Her boss, a woman she had respected, looked at her with visible frustration and said, “I need someone reliable, Leilani.” That night, she sat in her brightly lit living room, her husband asleep in the next room, and she realized she was losing pieces of herself she had not known she was holding. She did not know if she could trust me, or anyone, but she knew she could not go on like this. What she hoped for, though she could barely say it aloud, was to feel like she belonged somewhere again—even if that somewhere was just her own skin.
